Article continues below this ad
All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.

Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?

Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.

California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. Counties have been begging the state for permission to join a nonprofit, multistate organization that helps officials improve the accuracy of their voter rolls (https://apcp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-04/ab-2050-pellerin-apcp-analysis_1.pdf).

The California Motor Voter program is making registering to vote at the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) more convenient.
Eligible applicants completing a driver license, identification (ID) card or change of address transaction online, by mail or in person at the DMV will be automatically registered to vote by the California Secretary of State, unless they choose to opt out of automatic voter registration.

Since 1993, the National Voter Registration Act, often known as the Motor Voter law, has helped millions of people register to vote or update their voter information during a driver license or ID card transaction at the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV).
The California Motor Voter program applies to Californians who are 18 or older and meet the following criteria:
- A United States citizen and a resident of California.
- Not currently serving a state or federal prison term for the conviction of a felony (for more information on the rights of people who have been incarcerated, please see the Secretary of State's Voting Rights: Persons with a Criminal History), and
- Not currently found mentally incompetent to vote by a court (for more information, please see Voting Rights: Persons Subject to Conservatorship).

So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”

Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.

All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.

People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?

I'm examining signature rejection rates, funding sources, and court rulings on the ballot title. I'm also reviewing privacy concerns, implementation gaps, and polling data on voter ID access.

I am leaning toward a no vote. The evidence does not support a significant problem of voter impersonation or noncitizen voting at scale. Texas's similar law caused massive rejection of legitimate mail ballots. California already relies on mail voting for over 80 percent of votes, so this is a critical pathway. Requiring exact matching of the last four digits of a designated ID type creates a known failure mode. A constitutional amendment would also be difficult to fix if implementation goes badly.

The constitutional language is vague. It leaves too much to the legislature, which could stall implementation and trigger endless lawsuits.

The annual cost would be tens to hundreds of millions of dollars for a problem that is vanishingly rare. The Department of Justice has charged only 28 people and recovered 34 ballots out of 94 million since 2020, or roughly 0.00004 percent.

Supporters argue that public confidence in the election system is a legitimate democratic good even when fraud is rare. They also note that signature matching already rejects over 100,000 ballots and is error-prone. Some studies suggest voter ID laws have little effect on turnout.

Polling on voter ID has shifted. A Los Angeles Times poll in October 2026 found nearly six in ten oppose the measure.

I will not rely on editorial boards alone. I need to verify whether requiring ID numbers would reduce signature rejections or create a new failure mode. I also want to examine how California currently verifies citizenship at registration.

The text does not explicitly repeal signature requirements. It only mandates identity verification and single-ballot checks. I am also weighing whether the last four digits of a Social Security number on a mailed envelope actually prevents identity theft.

The constitutional text does not explicitly replace signature matching. Voters may face both signature and ID verification, creating an additional hurdle rather than a streamlined process.

The measure also requires existing voters to update their registration to designate a government-issued identification number. Those who fail to do so could be blocked from voting by mail.

The requirement would burden 22 million registered voters. Those who fail to update their records could be blocked from voting by mail in a state that relies on universal vote-by-mail. The text does note the designated ID type on the envelope, which may help voters locate the correct last four digits.

Texas provides a concrete warning. Voters who registered with a Social Security number but mistakenly use their driver's license will fail the ID check if they do not read the envelope carefully.

The last four digits of a Social Security number on the outside of a mail envelope is a known identity theft risk. Driver's license numbers are less sensitive but still personal information. Envelopes travel through the mail system and can be photographed or mishandled.

Signature matching is less vulnerable to identity theft than exposing the last four digits of a Social Security number, since the name and address are already on the envelope. The free voter ID card would not fully solve this. It requires a separate application, creates new state infrastructure, and leaves transaction costs. Voters who do not know about it or cannot obtain it before an election could still be blocked.

The constitutional definition of "government-issued identification" is ambiguous. It could include student IDs, utility bills, or passports. The legislature would need to clarify these details, but until then the law remains self-executing and open to litigation.

The citizenship verification requirement also relies on vague "best efforts" using government data. The SAVE database has known error rates. Matching voter rolls against citizenship records produces false positives from naturalized citizens and name mismatches.

The requirement to report annual verification percentages could pressure election officials to purge unverified voters. This would create a direct incentive for aggressive purges of eligible citizens, similar to the false-match removals seen in Georgia, Texas, and Kansas.

People registering to vote for the first time in California must check a box, under penalty of perjury, attesting that they are U.S. citizens who are eligible to vote.
Secretary of State Shirley Weber's office takes information presented by voters when they register, like their Social Security or driver's license number, and matches it to state records to verify a voter's identity.

So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”

Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.

All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. Counties have been begging the state for permission to join a nonprofit, multistate organization that helps officials improve the accuracy of their voter rolls (https://apcp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-04/ab-2050-pellerin-apcp-analysis_1.pdf).
But Prop 39 is a nakedly bad-faith effort designed to encourage frivolous lawsuits, deepen distrust, increase political polarization and waste taxpayer dollars. Vote no.

I have a solid picture of the proposition. I am gathering a few more pieces of evidence to be thorough.

Verifying the University of Maryland study on missing IDs. Checking Heritage Foundation fraud data and Kansas proof-of-citizenship results. Prop 39 lacks a cure process, unlike Texas. Reviewing the LA Times editorial recommendation and the ballot title lawsuit.

Checking PPIC poll data and the peer-reviewed Texas Journal of Politics study. The concern about last-four SSN on envelopes is legitimate but often overstated, since names and addresses are already present. The measure is self-executing, so it would prohibit voting without ID even if free voter IDs are not yet ready.

The self-executing clause would block voting immediately, before the state can pass implementing laws. Local elections occur before the next statewide election, so this creates a serious gap.

Checking the California Constitution to determine the exact effective date for this self-executing initiative. Article XVIII may specify a delay after election certification.

Article II Section 10 and Article XVIII Section 4 both specify that approved initiatives and constitutional amendments take effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of vote. This confirms the self-executing clause would not block voting immediately.

Prop 39 does not specify a delay, so it would take effect immediately after the Secretary of State certifies the vote. Local and special elections in early 2027 would be affected before the free voter ID system is ready. The measure also fails to define "government-issued identification" operationally, leaving counties to figure out how to verify last-four digits on mail ballots.

The measure requires voters to have already designated a government-issued identification number in their registration. Many voters have not done so, which would block their mail ballots under a strict reading. The LAO notes the Legislature must clarify these operational details.

The self-executing clause without a grace period risks invalidating large numbers of ballots and creating chaos. The measure also grants private citizens a broad right of action to sue counties for compliance, with no standing limits or fee-shifting rules specified. This invites serial litigation over the undefined "best efforts" standard for citizenship verification.

The YES side has two main arguments. First, public confidence in elections has declined, and PPIC polling shows 41 percent of voters worry about ineligible voting. A well-designed free voter ID could restore trust. Second, signature matching is flawed: over 70,000 ballots were rejected in 2024 for signature issues, disproportionately affecting young and Latino voters. A numeric ID match could be more objective and reduce false rejections if it replaces signatures and includes a robust cure process.

Prop 39 does not actually require replacing signatures or adding a cure process. Proponents claim it will reduce signature problems, but the text does not do that.

In-person voting currently does not verify signatures before counting. ID checks at polling places are reasonable against impersonation, though impersonation fraud is extremely rare according to Heritage and academic studies.

The cost of in-person ID verification with free cards would be lower than matching ID numbers on mail ballots in a universal vote-by-mail state.

The current system relies on attestation under penalty of perjury rather than documentary proof. The DMV does not maintain a comprehensive citizenship database, and some groups remain unverified. "Best efforts" reporting could be transparent without automatically purging ineligible voters, but the undefined standard combined with broad citizen lawsuits creates significant legal risk.

The State Auditor audit provision is a reasonable standalone good-government measure. Academic evidence on strict photo ID and turnout is mixed, with most studies finding near-zero effects. The closest relevant analog is Texas SB1, which required mail-ballot ID numbers and produced a rejection spike and reduced participation, especially among voters of color.

I have a solid picture of the proposition. I am gathering a few more pieces of evidence to be thorough.

Verifying the University of Maryland study on missing IDs. Checking Heritage Foundation fraud data and Kansas proof-of-citizenship results. Prop 39 lacks a cure process, unlike Texas. Reviewing the LA Times editorial recommendation and the ballot title lawsuit.

Checking PPIC poll data and the peer-reviewed Texas Journal of Politics study. The concern about last-four SSN on envelopes is legitimate but often overstated, since names and addresses are already present. The measure is self-executing, so it would prohibit voting without ID even if free voter IDs are not yet ready.

The self-executing clause would block voting immediately, before the state can pass implementing laws. Local elections occur before the next statewide election, so this creates a serious gap.

Checking the California Constitution to determine the exact effective date for this self-executing initiative. Article XVIII may specify a delay after election certification.

Article II Section 10 and Article XVIII Section 4 both specify that approved initiatives and constitutional amendments take effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of vote. This confirms the self-executing clause would not block voting immediately.

Prop 39 does not specify a delay, so it would take effect immediately after the Secretary of State certifies the vote. Local and special elections in early 2027 would be affected before the free voter ID system is ready. The measure also fails to define "government-issued identification" operationally, leaving counties to figure out how to verify last-four digits on mail ballots.

The measure requires voters to have already designated a government-issued identification number in their registration. Many voters have not done so, which would block their mail ballots under a strict reading. The LAO notes the Legislature must clarify these operational details.

The self-executing clause without a grace period risks invalidating large numbers of ballots and creating chaos. The measure also grants private citizens a broad right of action to sue counties for compliance, with no standing limits or fee-shifting rules specified. This invites serial litigation over the undefined "best efforts" standard for citizenship verification.

The YES side has two main arguments. First, public confidence in elections has declined, and PPIC polling shows 41 percent of voters worry about ineligible voting. A well-designed free voter ID could restore trust. Second, signature matching is flawed: over 70,000 ballots were rejected in 2024 for signature issues, disproportionately affecting young and Latino voters. A numeric ID match could be more objective and reduce false rejections if it replaces signatures and includes a robust cure process.

Prop 39 does not actually require replacing signatures or adding a cure process. Proponents claim it will reduce signature problems, but the text does not do that.

In-person voting currently does not verify signatures before counting. ID checks at polling places are reasonable against impersonation, though impersonation fraud is extremely rare according to Heritage and academic studies.

The cost of in-person ID verification with free cards would be lower than matching ID numbers on mail ballots in a universal vote-by-mail state.

The current system relies on attestation under penalty of perjury rather than documentary proof. The DMV does not maintain a comprehensive citizenship database, and some groups remain unverified. "Best efforts" reporting could be transparent without automatically purging ineligible voters, but the undefined standard combined with broad citizen lawsuits creates significant legal risk.

The State Auditor audit provision is a reasonable standalone good-government measure. Academic evidence on strict photo ID and turnout is mixed, with most studies finding near-zero effects. The closest relevant analog is Texas SB1, which required mail-ballot ID numbers and produced a rejection spike and reduced participation, especially among voters of color.

I have a thorough picture of the proposition. I am checking a few remaining details.

Prop 39 requires only best-efforts verification of citizenship attestations using government data. It does not mandate documentary proof at registration, unlike Kansas or Kobach's law. The UMD study about proof-of-citizenship documents is therefore less directly applicable.

The free voter ID card is not yet available, so the proposed system would be self-executing before it exists. Transaction costs remain. Most registered voters already have an ID number on file from registration, which helps mail voting.

Mail voting requires only the last four digits of a designated ID number, not a physical card. The small group of voters who registered without a driver's license or Social Security number would need the free voter ID card. Texas has shown that forgetting or mismatching that number is the bigger mail voting problem than lacking an ID. A court also found the proponents' claims that the measure makes voting easier and saves money to be false and misleading.

The judge also found the Attorney General's title accurately describes the measure's effect. It prohibits citizens from having their ballots counted unless they present government-issued identification.

California has seen roughly seventy heritage cases over more than forty years. The California Secretary of State found only six examples in 2020 through 2024. Most were caught and did not change election outcomes. This is not evidence of a systemic problem that this measure is designed to solve.

The Hawthorne and Compton cases involved candidate-driven registration fraud. Voter ID at the polls would not have prevented fictitious registrations. Fraudsters could still create fake IDs or vote by mail using controlled numbers. The 8,000 fake registrations in Hawthorne were caught before votes counted.

The Department of Justice charged twenty-eight people in 2026. Thirty-four ballots were alleged to be illegal out of roughly ninety-four million cast since 2020. The claim that twenty thousand noncitizens voted is unverified. Even if true it would be a small fraction of registered voters. Many may be database errors such as naturalized citizens or name collisions.

The measure's best-efforts verification could serve as a transparency tool. The private right of action makes it a litigation weapon.

I am now weighing the evidence to decide yes or no.

The decision is no. The harm is concrete and already documented. Texas provides the closest precedent: its mail ID number match law caused rejection rates to jump from roughly one percent to twelve percent in the first election, disproportionately affecting Black, Latino, and Asian voters. Even after an envelope redesign, rejections remained around three and a half percent, several times the prior rate. The benefit of this measure is speculative and small.

A peer-reviewed study found lasting turnout reductions. California votes eighty percent by mail, so this is the main effect.

Prop 39 requires an exact match to the designated ID number. The Attorney General summary explicitly warns that writing a different number than the one on file will not count the ballot. This is the exact Texas failure mode.

The constitutional text does not require a cure process. California's signature system has one, but this new requirement might not include it unless the legislature adds it. Even Texas had a cure and still threw out large numbers.

The existing system already verifies identity at registration, requires citizenship attestation under penalty of perjury, and allows voters to cure signature mismatches. Noncitizen voting is already a crime.

The Motor Voter Act excludes undocumented license applicants. The measure is poorly drafted as a constitutional amendment. It is self-executing with no delayed operative date, yet key terms are undefined and left to the legislature. The private right of action invites endless litigation. There is no clause allowing the legislature to amend the text, so fixing problems would require another constitutional amendment or a court.

The LAO estimates annual costs at tens of millions to hundreds of millions. The savings from fewer registrants likely would not exceed those costs. The fiscal savings include disenfranchising eligible voters who lack government-issued identification.

The free voter ID card would only help a small group of in-person voters if they know to request it, the system exists, and poll workers accept it. Studies show information barriers matter. The UK photo ID law turned away or dissuaded 1.2 to 2.4 percent of registered voters.

One in five California voting-age citizens lack a current driver's license with the correct name and address. Whether that blocks them depends on implementation rules the measure never specifies. Constitutional vagueness is itself a reason to reject the proposition.

The confidence argument is weak as justification for this specific text.

Voter ID may increase confidence in some studies, but large-scale rejection of valid ballots would likely decrease confidence among affected voters. The real sources of distrust are political messaging, not measured fraud. Audits and citizenship reporting could be passed by ordinary statute without this constitutional package.

Voting no does not prevent the legislature from improving signature curing, joining ERIC, or maintaining better voter lists.

The identity theft risk is real but secondary. A name, address, and last four digits of a Social Security number on a mailed envelope is more sensitive than a signature, yet the benefit remains weak.

A strong case for yes exists: most democracies and US states require some form of voter ID, and California is an outlier for in-person voting.

Signature matching rejects roughly seventy thousand ballots and is subjective. A number match could be fairer and faster if well implemented. Citizenship is a legal requirement, yet California officials often rely only on the voter's attestation. Annual verification reporting would add transparency. Free ID combined with mail voting is a milder design than strict photo ID or documentary proof of citizenship. Public support for the concept is high in general polls, though recent surveys show opposition once costs and disenfranchisement are described. Trust is a democratic good.

Forty-one percent of likely voters are concerned. The cost is less than 0.25 percent of the general fund. Rare fraud still dilutes legal votes, so deterrence has value. The legislature could implement this carefully with cure processes, broad acceptable IDs, and a phased rollout. Academic literature often finds small turnout effects from voter ID, so suppression fears may be overstated for in-person voting. The steelman argument fails because the mail-ballot ID number requirement is not the mild in-person ID that polls support.

The Texas precedent is especially relevant because California already votes by mail. The private right of action lets litigants demand the strictest reading, so the legislature cannot easily override the constitutional requirement. A cure process might be compatible, but it would likely not prevent the core rejection problem.

Even a modest rejection increase would discard roughly 130,000 to 260,000 valid ballots. That volume far exceeds the documented illegal votes. Locking in this poorly specified experiment is the wrong instrument. The answer is no.

The steelman argument fails because the mail-ballot ID number requirement is not the mild in-person ID that polls support.

The Texas precedent is especially relevant because California already votes by mail. The private right of action lets litigants demand the strictest reading, so the legislature cannot easily override the constitutional requirement. A cure process might be compatible, but it would likely not prevent the core rejection problem.

Even a modest rejection increase would discard roughly 130,000 to 260,000 valid ballots. That volume far exceeds the documented illegal votes. Locking in this poorly specified experiment is the wrong instrument. SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Fiscal Impact: Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.

**Sacramento, Calif.** – Today California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., made the November 3, 2026, California General Election Official Voter Information Guide available for public review.
The guide, which will be mailed to every voting household in California, includes information about propositions and statements from candidates running for constitutional offices, as well as other important election information such as the California Voter Bill of Rights and information about how eligible Californians can vote.
California’s Official Voter Information Guide is available in 10 languages—English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.
The guide is available for public examination from July 21, 2026 through August 10, 2026 at https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display and at the Office of the Secretary of State’s Sacramento and Los Angeles locations.
During this public display period, any elector can challenge any portion of the Official Voter Information Guide in Sacramento Superior Court.
Following the conclusion of the public examination period, the Office of the Secretary of State will begin printing and mailing the statewide Voter Information Guide to all households that have at least one registered voter.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.

Californians for Voter ID

PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.
Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter’s registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver’s license number on envelope, their ballot would not count).
Prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification.
Requires elections officials to annually report percentage of each county’s voters whose citizenship status they have verified.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.

PROPOSITION 39
This initiative measure is submitted to the people in
accordance with the provisions of Section 8 of Article II
of the California Constitution.
This initiative measure adds a section to the California
Constitution; therefore, new provisions proposed to be
added are printed in italic type to indicate that they are
new.
PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Findings and Purposes.
To enforce existing voter qualifications, including US
citizenship, established by California’s Constitution,
the people hereby amend the California Constitution:
(A) to promote public confidence and trust in the
electoral process, which encourages civic participation
and supports a healthy democracy; (B) to deter and
detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter
registration records and confirming eligibility to vote;
and (C) to minimize the risk of voter impersonation by
requiring proof of identity to vote.

### Abstract
Voter identification (ID) requirements are a contentious issue in the United States, yet inconsistent findings in existing research obscure whether these laws causally affect turnout.
This paper examines the differential impact of strict voter ID laws on midterm versus presidential elections and across early-adopting states (those that passed strict voter ID laws before the 2008
*Crawford v.
Marion County Election Board* decision) versus late-adopting states (those that adopted after 2008).
Using state-level turnout data from 1984 to 2020 and synthetic difference-in-differences to control for time-varying confounders, I find substantial heterogeneity in how states are affected.
While strict voter ID laws show no significant aggregate effect on turnout, disaggregated analysis reveals important variation: these laws decrease presidential election turnout by 2.7% in late-adopting states, while early-adopting states experience no significant effects.
Additionally, the laws appear to increase midterm election turnout by 2.9%, with this effect particularly pronounced among early-adopting states (3.3% increase).
These findings demonstrate that strict voter ID laws have heterogeneous effects that vary by election type and adoption timing, which may explain the conflicting results in prior research.

Texas provides a concrete warning. Voters who registered with a Social Security number but mistakenly use their driver's license will fail the ID check if they do not read the envelope carefully.

The last four digits of a Social Security number on the outside of a mail envelope is a known identity theft risk. Driver's license numbers are less sensitive but still personal information. Envelopes travel through the mail system and can be photographed or mishandled.

Signature matching is less vulnerable to identity theft than exposing the last four digits of a Social Security number, since the name and address are already on the envelope. The free voter ID card would not fully solve this. It requires a separate application, creates new state infrastructure, and leaves transaction costs. Voters who do not know about it or cannot obtain it before an election could still be blocked.

The constitutional definition of "government-issued identification" is ambiguous. It could include student IDs, utility bills, or passports. The legislature would need to clarify these details, but until then the law remains self-executing and open to litigation.

The citizenship verification requirement also relies on vague "best efforts" using government data. The SAVE database has known error rates. Matching voter rolls against citizenship records produces false positives from naturalized citizens and name mismatches.

The requirement to report annual verification percentages could pressure election officials to purge unverified voters. This would create a direct incentive for aggressive purges of eligible citizens, similar to the false-match removals seen in Georgia, Texas, and Kansas.

So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”

Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.

All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.

People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?

Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.

I have a solid picture of the proposition. I am gathering a few more pieces of evidence to be thorough.

Verifying the University of Maryland study on missing IDs. Checking Heritage Foundation fraud data and Kansas proof-of-citizenship results. Prop 39 lacks a cure process, unlike Texas. Reviewing the LA Times editorial recommendation and the ballot title lawsuit.

Checking PPIC poll data and the peer-reviewed Texas Journal of Politics study. The concern about last-four SSN on envelopes is legitimate but often overstated, since names and addresses are already present. The measure is self-executing, so it would prohibit voting without ID even if free voter IDs are not yet ready.

The self-executing clause would block voting immediately, before the state can pass implementing laws. Local elections occur before the next statewide election, so this creates a serious gap.

Checking the California Constitution to determine the exact effective date for this self-executing initiative. Article XVIII may specify a delay after election certification.

Article II Section 10 and Article XVIII Section 4 both specify that approved initiatives and constitutional amendments take effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of vote. This confirms the self-executing clause would not block voting immediately.

Prop 39 does not specify a delay, so it would take effect immediately after the Secretary of State certifies the vote. Local and special elections in early 2027 would be affected before the free voter ID system is ready. The measure also fails to define "government-issued identification" operationally, leaving counties to figure out how to verify last-four digits on mail ballots.

The measure requires voters to have already designated a government-issued identification number in their registration. Many voters have not done so, which would block their mail ballots under a strict reading. The LAO notes the Legislature must clarify these operational details.

The self-executing clause without a grace period risks invalidating large numbers of ballots and creating chaos. The measure also grants private citizens a broad right of action to sue counties for compliance, with no standing limits or fee-shifting rules specified. This invites serial litigation over the undefined "best efforts" standard for citizenship verification.

The YES side has two main arguments. First, public confidence in elections has declined, and PPIC polling shows 41 percent of voters worry about ineligible voting. A well-designed free voter ID could restore trust. Second, signature matching is flawed: over 70,000 ballots were rejected in 2024 for signature issues, disproportionately affecting young and Latino voters. A numeric ID match could be more objective and reduce false rejections if it replaces signatures and includes a robust cure process.

Prop 39 does not actually require replacing signatures or adding a cure process. Proponents claim it will reduce signature problems, but the text does not do that.

In-person voting currently does not verify signatures before counting. ID checks at polling places are reasonable against impersonation, though impersonation fraud is extremely rare according to Heritage and academic studies.

The cost of in-person ID verification with free cards would be lower than matching ID numbers on mail ballots in a universal vote-by-mail state.

The current system relies on attestation under penalty of perjury rather than documentary proof. The DMV does not maintain a comprehensive citizenship database, and some groups remain unverified. "Best efforts" reporting could be transparent without automatically purging ineligible voters, but the undefined standard combined with broad citizen lawsuits creates significant legal risk.

The State Auditor audit provision is a reasonable standalone good-government measure. Academic evidence on strict photo ID and turnout is mixed, with most studies finding near-zero effects. The closest relevant analog is Texas SB1, which required mail-ballot ID numbers and produced a rejection spike and reduced participation, especially among voters of color.

The research, conducted by the nonpartisan nonprofit VoteRiders in partnership with the University of Maryland, takes a closer look at who in California lacks a current driver’s license, state ID, or proof of U.S. citizenship.

“I think a big key takeaway is significant percentages of eligible voters lack the type of ID and proof of citizenship documents that are increasingly required to vote in elections across the country,” said Lauren Kunis, CEO of VoteRiders.
"One in five Californians, so that's 4.5 million U.S. citizens of voting age, do not have a current driver's license with up-to-date information on it."
